ut.title: Ultrasonic Thickness Testing & UT Inspection, Jacksonville
ut.description: UT inspection in Jacksonville, FL: wall thickness surveys and ultrasonic weld examination for river terminals, ship repair, mills and bridges. Get a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) and Thickness Inspection in Jacksonville, Florida
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT provides ultrasonic testing in Jacksonville, Florida, covering wall thickness surveys on tanks, vessels, piping and ship structure and ultrasonic examination of welds. Work is carried out for terminals along the St. Johns River, shipyards and repair berths, industrial plants and steel structures across Duval County. Technicians travel to your site for an agreed scope. Describe the components in the UT inspection quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Jacksonville

Jacksonville's economy is built around the river and the port. JAXPORT's marine terminals at Blount Island, Talleyrand and Dames Point handle containers, vehicles, heavy lift, breakbulk steel and paper, forest products and liquid bulk such as molasses and vegetable oils, and the harbor also holds more than twenty privately operated facilities including drydocks and petroleum terminals. The city also hosts major military installations. Every one of those activities depends on steel that corrodes in a warm, wet, brackish environment.

  • Liquid bulk and petroleum tanks: shell, roof and nozzle thickness on vertical tanks that store fuels, edible oils and molasses.
  • Ship repair and drydock work: hull plate gauging, tank boundary plating and piping on vessels coming in for repair, where thickness drives steel renewal decisions.
  • Heavy-lift and container cranes: thickness of structural members and examination of welds at fatigue-prone details.
  • Industrial plants: boilers, digesters, process vessels and steam piping in forest-products, food and chemical plants around the city.
  • Bridges and structures: the many river and creek crossings and elevated structures where steel girders, bearings and connections need periodic checks.
  • Rail and intermodal yards: equipment and structures serving the rail connections to the port terminals.

Brackish water makes the picture more severe than a freshwater site. The St. Johns River is tidal for a long way upstream, and splash zones, pilings, ballast tanks and the lowest courses of shoreline tanks all see wet-dry cycles that attack coatings and steel unevenly.

What ultrasonic testing finds and what it misses

UT works by sending a short pulse of high-frequency sound into steel and timing its echo from the back wall or from a flaw. For corrosion work it gives remaining wall thickness at a point. For welds, an angled beam passes through the volume of the joint and reports reflectors such as lack of fusion, incomplete penetration, cracks and slag inclusions.

The technique is strong where access is good and the surface is sound, and weaker in other conditions. A pitted or heavily scaled surface may need cleaning before the probe will couple. A coating that has disbonded from the steel can hide a thin spot, since sound reflects at the gap. A single reading can miss a local pit between two points, so grids are sized to the corrosion pattern expected. Coarse-grained castings and some stainless welds scatter sound and reduce what can be reliably examined. When the beam cannot cover part of a joint, the report states the uncovered portion rather than implying full coverage.

Codes and acceptance criteria used in Jacksonville

The procedure is based on ASME Section V. Article 4 covers ultrasonic examination of welds, Article 5 covers materials, and thickness measurement appears in SE-797, which is in Article 23. The accept or reject limits come from the code that governs the item:

  1. Vessels built to ASME Section VIII Division 1 use Mandatory Appendix 12 for ultrasonic examination of welds.
  2. Process and power piping fall under ASME B31.3 (examination in paragraph 344.6, criteria in Table 341.3.2) or ASME B31.1.
  3. Aboveground storage tanks in service are inspected under API 653, supported by API RP 575 for storage tank practices.
  4. Structural steel is examined under AWS D1.1 for buildings and AWS D1.5 for bridges, which is the code that state transportation agencies apply to steel highway bridges.
  5. ASTM E797 describes contact pulse-echo thickness measurement, and ASTM E164 covers contact ultrasonic examination of weldments.

The owner's authorized inspector is responsible for inspection under API 510, 570 and 653; Atlantis gathers the thickness and weld data and reports it. In Florida the state boiler law, chapter 554 of the Florida Statutes, adds certificate inspections for covered boilers through the Department of Financial Services, and UT results on a boiler are data for that inspector.

How the thickness survey is run

The job starts with a scope: which lines, vessels or tank courses, and at which locations. A grid or condition monitoring location list is established from drawings and, where available, earlier survey data, so the same points are measured again. On the day of the work the instrument is calibrated on a step block of matching material. For corroded steel a dual-element probe is used, and the technician reads the A-scan instead of a bare digital number, which avoids errors on thin or pitted wall, including a reading that is double the real thickness.

Hot lines call for a high-temperature probe and couplant and a correction for temperature. Tank shells in Jacksonville summers are warm to the touch, and surfaces in sun are hotter. The procedure sets limits and corrections for these conditions, and the calibration is checked again at intervals through the shift and at the end.

How welds are examined

Weld examination uses shear-wave angle-beam probes, with angles such as 45, 60 and 70 degrees chosen for the thickness and joint type. A reference level or a distance-amplitude curve is built from side-drilled holes in a calibration block. The technician scans along and across the weld, evaluates any indication against the curve and records its length, depth and position. Planar flaws such as cracks and lack of fusion are judged against stricter limits than rounded flaws. For critical welds the procedure specifies a scan from both sides and the weld surface condition required.

Weld caps that are rough or reinforcement that is high can prevent a proper scan, and the owner may need to dress the weld. The scope can allow for light grinding to be done by others before the examination.

Who does the work and under what rules

Level II technicians perform and interpret the examination under Atlantis's written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. An ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. Level III oversight comes from Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, and the company is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. If a shipyard, terminal operator or customer requires its own written practice or procedure format, written practice development or Level III consulting can align the paperwork before work begins.

Hull plate, ballast tanks and other ship-side work

Ship repair in the harbor adds a thickness job that land plants rarely see. Hull plating wastes unevenly: the waterline belt, the bottom plating over ballast tanks, the plating around sea chests and the tank boundaries below cargo spaces all lose steel at different rates. A hull gauging plan therefore follows the ship's own structure, with readings taken on each plate between frames and across the stiffeners, so the renewal decision rests on the plates that are actually thin and not on an average.

Gauging is usually done after the surface has been cleaned by the yard, and from inside ballast tanks the work is a confined space job with ventilation, gas tests and a standby person. Readings from a tank's bottom plates, for example, are taken from inside while the vessel is afloat or docked. The report is organized by frame and plate so that the repair supervisor can mark up renewals directly from it. Class society surveys are a separate matter from an owner's own condition gauging, and the owner or the society decides what each reading is used for.

Bridges, girders and fracture-critical steel

Jacksonville sits on a river with many crossings, and steel highway and rail structures there are examined under bridge-specific rules. Ultrasonic examination of bridge steel is usually applied to groove welds in girders and to repair welds, and thickness readings check section loss on flanges, webs and bearing stiffeners where water collects. The owner's bridge program, not the inspection firm, determines which members are fracture critical and how often they are visited. Lane closures, rigging and traffic control are the owner's to arrange, so the plan should allow time for them before technicians mobilize.

What the report gives you

A UT report identifies each component and location, then lists the procedure and revision, instrument, probes, calibration blocks and calibration checks, surface condition and temperature, and the technician and level. Thickness is reported by location in a table or on a grid sketch with nominal and minimum required values for comparison, so loss rates can be calculated. Weld indications are listed with position, length, depth and amplitude and given an accept or reject decision against the named criterion. Limitations, such as an area that could not be reached, appear in plain words. A tank or hull report often includes a plate map so renewals can be planned from it.

Planning a UT job in Jacksonville

Jacksonville weather and logistics shape the work. Summers are hot and humid with frequent afternoon thunderstorms, and lightning stops work at height or on tank roofs. Hurricane season runs from June to November, and the river and port close to traffic during storms, which can reshuffle access to terminals and drydocks. Winters are mild, so cold is rarely a limit.

Access takes planning. Port terminals need identification and orientation, shipyards and drydocks have their own safety rules, and tanks and confined spaces need permits and gas tests. Ship work is usually scheduled around the vessel's time alongside, so a UT plan agreed before the vessel arrives gives the repair team data when they need it. Atlantis has no office in Jacksonville; technicians are mobilized from outside the area and travel is part of the quote.

UT, MT or PT for your Jacksonville job

If the question is wall loss or an internal weld flaw, UT is the method. If the question is a surface crack in carbon steel, magnetic particle inspection in Jacksonville is faster. If the metal is stainless or aluminum, or you need to find any surface-breaking flaw, choose liquid penetrant testing in Jacksonville. The national ultrasonic testing page and the Florida inspection hub give more context, and the ultrasonic testing guide explains the method in depth.

Building your own UT team

Owners with a steady workload may prefer in-house inspectors. UT Level 1 and UT Level 2 courses are available, with a browser UT simulator for practice and a page on NDT training in Jacksonville. Under SNT-TC-1A your company certifies the technician after the training and experience hours are met.

faq.q: Does Atlantis staff an office in Jacksonville?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Jacksonville. Technicians are mobilized to your terminal, yard, plant or project site for the agreed scope, and travel is included in the quote. We reply within one business day.

faq.q: Can UT be done on a ship while it is in a Jacksonville drydock or alongside?
faq.a: Yes, subject to access and safety rules. Hull plate and tank boundary readings can be taken once surfaces are cleaned and staging is in place. The vessel schedule normally sets the window, so share it with the request.

faq.q: How is thickness measured on a brackish-water tank or piling?
faq.a: Surface scale and marine growth are removed, a couplant is applied and a dual-element probe is read against a calibrated step block. Pitted areas are checked on the A-scan so that false readings are caught.

faq.q: Which standards apply to UT weld examination on structural steel?
faq.a: Technique follows ASME Section V Article 4. For buildings the acceptance criteria are in AWS D1.1, while AWS D1.5 governs steel highway bridges. Pressure vessels and piping use ASME Section VIII or B31.3.

faq.q: Does UT replace the Florida boiler inspection?
faq.a: No. Covered boilers receive certificate inspections under Florida chapter 554 from certified boiler inspectors. UT thickness data supports the inspector and the owner but is not a statutory inspection.

faq.q: What happens when a thickness reading is below the minimum?
faq.a: The reading is reported straight away to your authorized inspector or engineer, with its location and the surrounding readings. The owner decides on repair, derating or a shorter inspection interval; Atlantis supplies the evidence.

faq.q: Does Atlantis serve as the API 653 inspector of record?
faq.a: No. The owner-appointed authorized inspector remains inspector of record under API 653. Atlantis carries out the ultrasonic examination and gives that inspector the thickness data and records.

faq.q: What should I send to get a UT quote in Jacksonville?
faq.a: List the components, materials, thicknesses, operating temperature, coating, access method, governing code and any site or vessel schedule. Send them through the quote form and we reply within one business day.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) | Jacksonville, FL
mt.description: Mag particle testing in Jacksonville, FL for crane welds, ship repair steel, bridge connections and mill equipment, mobilized to your site. Request a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Jacksonville, Florida
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT performs magnetic particle inspection (MT), also known as mag particle testing or MPI, in Jacksonville, Florida. It finds surface and near-surface cracks in ferromagnetic steel: welds on heavy-lift cranes, repair welds on ships in the harbor, bridge and structural connections, and rotating or lifting equipment in industrial plants. Technicians travel to the site once the scope is agreed. Send the details through the MT inspection quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle testing is used in Jacksonville

Jacksonville moves enormous tonnage across its docks. JAXPORT lists autos, containers, heavy lift, breakbulk, forest products, liquid bulk and military cargo among its handling categories, and each category relies on steel equipment that is loaded, vibrated and welded repeatedly. Magnetic particle inspection is the quick check that catches the crack before it becomes a failure.

  • Heavy-lift and container cranes: welds at boom hinges, trolley frames, spreader connections and the base of pedestals, where cyclic loading starts fatigue cracks.
  • Rigging and lifting gear: hooks, shackles, lifting lugs, pins and beams, which are examined periodically and after any overload event.
  • Ship repair: repair welds on frames, stiffeners, rudder and propulsion supports, and weld toes around renewed plating inside the drydocks and repair berths of the harbor.
  • Bridge and structural steel: fracture-critical members, gusset plates and welded connections on the many spans over the river and creeks, examined under bridge welding rules.
  • Industrial plants: lifting attachments and support welds on vessels and tanks, and heavy machinery in mills and processing plants.
  • Rail equipment and track structures: couplers, frames and welds on equipment serving the intermodal yards.

Moisture is the quiet enemy. Brackish air accelerates corrosion on weld toes and at bolted connections, and pitting at a toe is a ready-made stress riser that cracks under load. A crack at that location often hides under corrosion product until it is cleaned away.

What MT detects and what it cannot

When a ferromagnetic part is magnetized, a surface or near-surface discontinuity such as a crack, lap or lack of fusion interrupts the magnetic flux and leaks it into the air. Fine particles dusted or sprayed on the surface are caught at the leakage and outline the flaw in seconds. The result is a direct visual picture of the crack, its length and its orientation.

MT cannot examine nonmagnetic metals such as austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper or bronze. It is not a volumetric method, so it will miss flaws buried deeper than a small fraction of an inch. It also depends on direction: a crack lying along the field direction produces a weak or no indication, which is why two examinations at roughly right angles are standard. Thick coatings, heavy rust and sharp geometry change weaken or confuse the pattern, and the technician must distinguish true cracks from nonrelevant indications at section changes.

Standards and acceptance for MT jobs in Jacksonville

The technique rests on ASME Section V Article 7, with ASTM E1444 as the practice and ASTM E709 as a guide. The criteria applied are those of the governing code:

  1. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Mandatory Appendix 6 for vessel welds.
  2. ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 and Table 341.3.2 for process piping, and B31.1 for power piping.
  3. AWS D1.1 for structural steel, where visual and MT results are judged against weld profile and crack limits, and AWS D1.5 for bridge steel under state transportation agency contracts.
  4. API 510, 570 and 653 for in-service equipment, where the owner's authorized inspector remains responsible for the inspection and Atlantis delivers the examination data.

Lifting equipment may also fall under the equipment manufacturer's instructions and the owner's rigging program, and those documents are read and cited in the procedure.

How magnetic particle examination is performed

Preparation precedes everything. The area is cleaned of grease, loose scale and paint, and the contrast of the surface against the particles is checked. For field work the usual magnetizing tool is an electromagnetic yoke with articulated legs. Section V Article 7 sets the minimum lifting power at 10 pounds for an AC yoke and 40 pounds for a DC or permanent-magnet yoke, at the largest pole spacing used, and the yoke is lift-tested before use.

The steps run in a fixed order:

  1. Verify the equipment, the particle suspension or powder and the lighting.
  2. Magnetize the area with the yoke legs straddling the weld or suspect zone.
  3. Apply particles while the field is on, and examine while the particles are still mobile.
  4. Rotate the yoke about 90 degrees and repeat so that cracks in any direction are caught.
  5. Demagnetize if the part's use requires it, and clean the particles off.

Visible dry powder is common outdoors on rough, warm surfaces. Wet visible or fluorescent particles give more sensitivity, and fluorescent work is viewed under UV-A light in a darkened area, which on a bright Jacksonville day means a tent or a shaded enclosure. A field indicator or a reference piece confirms the direction and strength of the field.

What the indications look like

A true crack on a wet or dry MT inspection appears as a sharp, tight line, often crooked, that builds up as the field is held and stays when the particles are lightly disturbed. A weld toe crack runs along the edge of the weld. A crater crack at the end of a weld star-shapes. A fatigue crack in a hook or a pin follows the root of a thread or a corner. Nonrelevant indications look different: they are broad and fuzzy, and appear at changes of section, at the edge of a heat-affected zone or along a magnetic writing where two pieces touch.

When the technician is unsure, the standard moves are to wipe the area, magnetize again at a different angle and compare. If the indication returns the same way, it is measured and evaluated. If it disappears, the cause is noted. Doubtful cases go to the Level III, and nothing is signed off as clean on a guess.

Surface preparation and recoating

Preparation on a Jacksonville job is usually a matter of removing salt crust, marine growth, flaking coatings and weld spatter with a wire brush or a grinder. The technician checks that the surface is dry, because water changes how particles move. Thin intact coatings can stay when the procedure covers them, but thick ones come off locally. After examination the surface is wiped clean of particles. Because bare steel starts rusting quickly in this climate, the owner's coating crew should be ready to recoat soon after the report is issued.

Lifting gear, repair history and record keeping

Owners of lifting gear get the most from MT when the examination is tied to the equipment's history. Each hook, pin or lug has a serial number or tag, and the report ties the result to it, so a later examination can show whether a mark was present last time and whether it has grown. A part that fails, or is repaired by welding, is re-examined after the repair and again after any load test, and all three results sit in the same file. For heavy-lift equipment that moves between jobs, that file becomes the proof an owner or a customer asks to see.

The owner decides what to do with a rejected component. Atlantis reports the finding and the criterion it failed; replacement, repair procedure and return-to-service approval stay with the owner and the engineer or manufacturer responsible for the equipment.

Who performs the work

MT is performed by Level II technicians qualified under Atlantis's written practice, which is based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Procedures are approved by an ASNT Level III, Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. Customers who have their own procedure format can use Level III consulting to align it, and the national magnetic particle testing page covers the service in general.

What the MT report contains

Each report names the component, its tag or drawing reference and location, the procedure and revision, the equipment and its calibration or lift-test status, the particle type, the lighting measurements and the surface condition. Indications are recorded with location, orientation and length, supported by sketches or photographs, and marked accepted or rejected against the code criterion. After a repair the area is re-examined and added to the same report, so the sequence of original crack, repair and final clean result stays in one document.

Wet or dry particles for Jacksonville conditions

The choice between particle forms is made by the surface and the weather. Dry powder is easy to carry and works on warm, rough steel such as a crane boom, but it loses mobility in damp air. Wet visible particles in an oil or water carrier give a smoother, more sensitive pattern on cleaned welds. Wet fluorescent particles are the most sensitive and suit critical welds, provided a dark enclosure can be set up. The procedure states which form applies to which component, and the technician records the particle concentration check that proves the suspension is working.

Planning an MT job in Jacksonville

Hot, humid summers and thunderstorms dominate the planning. Steel in the sun can run well above air temperature, so part temperature is checked against the procedure's limits, and shaded or early work is sensible for exposed structures. Dry powder clumps in damp air, which is a reason to prefer wet particles during the wet season. Lightning and wind interrupt crane and rigging work, and during hurricane season the port and shipyards shift to storm preparation.

Access follows the site's rules: port credentials, safety orientation, permits for confined spaces and hot work, and the vessel or equipment schedule. Bridge work adds traffic control and lane closures arranged by the owner. Atlantis has no office in Jacksonville, so technicians are mobilized from outside the area and travel appears in the quote.

MT, PT or UT for your Jacksonville job

Use MT for surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel, particularly in welds and lifting gear. Use liquid penetrant testing in Jacksonville for nonmagnetic metals and for any clean, non-porous surface. Use ultrasonic testing in Jacksonville where wall loss or internal weld flaws are the concern. A repair can need all three: UT to define the thin area, MT on the new welds and PT on the stainless fittings. Further reading is available in the magnetic particle testing guide, the Article 7 explainer and on the Florida inspection hub.

Training your own MT technicians

Maintenance departments and shipyards that inspect gear regularly may choose to train their own people. MT Level 1 and MT Level 2 courses are offered, as is the magnetic particle testing training overview and the NDT training in Jacksonville page. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer completes the qualification and certification.

faq.q: What materials can be examined by magnetic particle inspection in Jacksonville?
faq.a: Only ferromagnetic materials such as carbon and low-alloy steel. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper and bronze are not magnetic, so those metals are examined by liquid penetrant testing instead.

faq.q: How often should crane hooks and rigging gear be checked with MT?
faq.a: The interval is set by the manufacturer, the owner rigging program and the applicable standard, and checks are usually repeated after overload events. MT is one tool in that program, alongside visual checks and load tests.

faq.q: Can magnetic particle inspection be done through paint?
faq.a: Thin, well-bonded coatings may be left on if the procedure demonstrated that indications still show through them. Thicker or flaking coatings and heavy rust are removed locally before the examination.

faq.q: Why does the yoke need a lift test before use?
faq.a: Section V Article 7 requires an AC yoke to lift at least 10 pounds and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds at the maximum pole spacing. The lift test proves the field strength is adequate before any weld is examined.

faq.q: Does Atlantis examine bridge welds in Jacksonville?
faq.a: Atlantis performs MT and UT on welded steel to the code the owner specifies, including AWS D1.5 for highway bridges. Traffic control, access equipment and owner approval of the procedure are arranged by the bridge owner.

faq.q: Does humidity affect magnetic particle testing on the coast?
faq.a: Yes. Dry powder clumps and loses mobility in damp air, and wet surfaces can disturb the test. Wet particles or shaded, drier working windows are often chosen for Jacksonville jobs in the summer.

faq.q: Is demagnetization needed after MT?
faq.a: It is needed if leftover magnetism could affect later welding, machining, instruments or bearings. The part is checked with a gauss meter, and the requirement is written into the scope and the report.

faq.q: How can I request MT inspection in Jacksonville?
faq.a: Use the quote form with the parts, steel type, coating condition, location, access, governing code and site requirements. Atlantis has no office in Jacksonville, technicians travel to you, and we reply within one business day.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Jacksonville, FL
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing in Jacksonville, FL for stainless tanks and piping, marine fittings, aluminum and weld repairs, mobilized to site. Request a quote.
pt.h1: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Jacksonville, Florida
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT carries out dye penetrant inspection, also called liquid penetrant testing or PT, in Jacksonville, Florida. It shows cracks, laps, seams and pinholes that are open to the surface of any clean, non-porous metal, which makes it the working method for stainless tanks, aluminum, bronze marine fittings and nickel alloys. Technicians travel to the site for the work. Send the part list through the PT inspection quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where liquid penetrant testing is used in Jacksonville

The same harbor that brings steel to Jacksonville also brings the metals that magnets cannot examine. Liquid bulk terminals store vegetable oils and molasses in stainless or lined tanks. Food and beverage processing uses sanitary stainless pipe and vessels. Ship repair handles bronze valves and propellers, aluminum structures and stainless fittings. Plants use stainless and nickel alloys for corrosive service. In all those settings a surface-breaking crack is the failure to find, and penetrant testing finds it.

Jacksonville components often examined by liquid penetrant testing
ComponentMaterialSurface-breaking concern
Edible-oil and food-grade tank seamsAustenitic stainless steelWeld cracks and pinholes that harbor contamination or leak
Propellers, shafts, valve bodiesBronze, stainless, cast steelFatigue cracks and casting defects found during repair
Aluminum deck and superstructure weldsAluminum alloysCrater cracks and toe cracks after repair welding
Process piping branch weldsStainless and nickel alloysCracks at socket and branch connections
Weld repair groovesAny weldable metalResidual cracks before rewelding

Hygiene gives PT extra weight in food service. A hairline crack in a sanitary vessel can trap product and defeat cleaning, so some owners examine key welds even though no code requires it.

What penetrant testing detects and where it stops

Penetrant is drawn into a surface-breaking flaw by capillary action. After the excess is removed, a developer draws the liquid back out and spreads it into a visible stain, magnified so a crack a fraction of a millimeter wide can be seen. Because it relies on the flaw being open to the surface, PT cannot see subsurface flaws or wall loss. A flaw smeared closed by grinding, peening or blasting may be missed unless the surface is etched or conditioned, and a surface sealed with paint, oil or dirt will not accept penetrant. Rough castings and porous surfaces trap liquid and produce background that obscures fine indications.

Codes, practices and acceptance criteria

The written procedure uses ASME Section V Article 6 and ASTM E165, and acceptance follows the governing code:

  • ASME Section VIII Division 1, Mandatory Appendix 8, for welds and surfaces on pressure vessels.
  • ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 and Table 341.3.2 for process piping, and B31.1 for power piping.
  • AWS D1.1 for structural welds, AWS D1.5 for bridges and AWS D1.6 for stainless steel structures.
  • API 510 and API 570 programs, where the owner's authorized inspector is responsible and the examination data comes from Atlantis.

Article 6 limits the halogen and sulfur content of penetrant materials used on austenitic stainless steel and nickel alloys, and requires the results to be documented. That limit is relevant to Jacksonville's stainless tanks and piping, which also sit in a humid, chloride-bearing marine atmosphere.

How the penetrant examination is carried out

The sequence is strict, and each step affects the next:

  1. Preparation: remove paint, scale, oil, spatter and corrosion, then clean with a solvent and let the surface dry fully.
  2. Penetrant application: brush, spray or dip, and keep the surface wet for the dwell time stated in the procedure.
  3. Excess removal: wipe with a dry cloth, then with a cloth lightly dampened with remover; flooding the surface with solvent washes penetrant out of flaws.
  4. Development: apply a thin, even coat of developer and wait the specified time.
  5. Examination: inspect under adequate light, record indications and, where needed, clean and retest.

Visible red penetrants with solvent removal and nonaqueous developer are the usual field choice. Fluorescent systems, viewed under UV-A light, serve when sensitivity matters more than convenience and the area can be darkened. The system is fixed by the procedure and is not changed halfway through a job.

Penetrant families and choosing among them

Penetrant materials are classed by type, method and sensitivity in ASTM E165. Type I uses a fluorescent dye viewed under UV-A light, and Type II uses a visible dye viewed in white light. The method defines how excess is removed: water-washable, post-emulsified or solvent-removable. Fluorescent systems at high sensitivity find the finest cracks but need darkness and are fussier on rough surfaces.

On Jacksonville job sites the choice is practical. A solvent-removable visible system fits a tank farm or a ship's deck, where there is no water supply and no dark booth. A water-washable fluorescent system fits a repair shop that handles many cast or machined parts. Whatever the choice, the procedure names it, and the technician does not mix products from different families on the same surface, since the residue of one can ruin the sensitivity of another.

Interpreting what the developer shows

The developer turns a trace of penetrant into a visible mark, and the technician has to decide what the mark means. A sharp red line that grows slowly is a crack or a lap. A cluster of dots is porosity. A broad stain along a scratch or a thread root is usually nonrelevant. Codes classify an indication as linear when its length is more than three times its width, and linear indications are judged more strictly than rounded ones.

In stainless steel exposed to warm, humid and chloride-bearing air, surface stress corrosion cracking can appear as a fine branching network that the eye cannot see, and penetrant testing is the method that reveals it. In aluminum repair welds, crater cracks at the end of a pass are a typical finding. Borderline indications are recorded, and the technician repeats the cleaning and retest instead of guessing.

Safety, solvents and waste

Penetrant products are chemicals and the sites they are used on have rules for them. Cleaners and developers in aerosol form are flammable, so hot work permits and nearby ignition sources affect when work starts. Closed tanks need ventilation and entry controls before solvent is used. Safety data sheets are reviewed with site staff before the first can is opened, and used wipes and empty cans are collected and disposed of as the site requires. Where a part goes into oxygen or other reactive service, the scope includes a final cleaning step and a cleanliness check.

Pre-cleaning, post-cleaning and keeping stainless clean

Cleaning matters twice on stainless work. Before the test, the surface must be free of anything that could plug a flaw. After the test, penetrant residue and developer are removed so that nothing remains to attract contamination or interfere with later coating, welding or product contact. For sanitary vessels the scope names the final rinse and the check that the surface is clean. Carbon steel tools and wire brushes are kept away from stainless surfaces, since embedded iron particles can rust and spoil a clean weld. Where this detail is left out of a scope, it is better to ask than to assume.

Who performs the work

Penetrant examinations are performed by Level II personnel qualified under Atlantis's written practice, based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, while an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. That role is held by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. Owners who need a procedure matched to their own specification can use Level III consulting, and the national penetrant testing page describes the service generally.

What the PT report records

The report identifies the part, its tag and location, the procedure and revision, and the penetrant materials by type, method, manufacturer and batch, with contaminant data for stainless or nickel alloy work. It records surface preparation, part temperature, dwell and development times, lighting and the technician and level. Each indication is described by location, size and whether it is linear or rounded, with a photograph or sketch and an accept or reject decision against the code. Where a flaw is repaired, the retest is recorded in the same file.

Checking that the penetrant system is working

A penetrant examination is only as good as the materials, so system performance is verified. A known-defect comparator block, a plate with fine cracks in a standard pattern, is used to show that the system reveals the finest flaws it should. The technician also checks that the materials are within their date, from the same family and not contaminated by earlier use. If the comparator shows poor results, the examination is stopped and the system is replaced or rechecked. These checks take minutes and are recorded in the report.

Planning a PT job in Jacksonville

Penetrant testing is the most temperature-sensitive of the three conventional methods. The standard range under Section V Article 6 for the part and the materials is 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Jacksonville's mild winters keep cold in range most of the time, but a dark steel or stainless surface in summer sun can be well above 125 degrees, and outside the range the procedure must be qualified at the actual temperature. Plan work in shade, in the cooler hours or inside a tent.

Humidity, dew and rain contaminate a prepared surface and dilute penetrant, so weather decides the schedule. Hot work and flammable solvent rules at fuel and food-grade plants affect timing, and confined tank interiors require ventilation and permits. Used wipes, cans and rinse liquids are collected as waste under the site's rules. Atlantis has no office in Jacksonville; technicians travel to the site and the quote covers travel.

Owners sometimes ask whether PT can be used on a weld that has just been ground. It can, provided the grinding did not smear metal over a crack; if smearing is suspected, light etching or a different preparation is specified first.

PT, MT or UT for your Jacksonville job

Choose PT for stainless, aluminum, bronze and nickel alloys and for any surface that must be proved free of open cracks. For carbon steel welds, magnetic particle inspection in Jacksonville is quicker. For wall loss and internal weld flaws, use ultrasonic testing in Jacksonville. A comparison of the methods is in the MT versus PT guide, the Article 6 explainer and the Florida inspection hub.

Training your own PT technicians

PT is quick to learn, and owners of stainless plants and repair yards often train their own staff. PT Level 1 and PT Level 2 courses are offered, along with the penetrant testing training overview, a PT simulator and the Jacksonville training page. The employer certifies under SNT-TC-1A.

faq.q: Can dye penetrant testing be used on bronze propellers and aluminum structures?
faq.a: Yes. Penetrant testing works on any clean, non-porous metal, including bronze, aluminum and stainless steel. Magnetic particle inspection cannot examine these nonmagnetic metals, so PT is the usual surface method for them.

faq.q: What does penetrant testing miss?
faq.a: It misses anything not open to the surface, such as internal flaws and wall loss, and flaws closed by smearing, paint or dirt. Ultrasonic testing covers wall loss and internal weld flaws.

faq.q: Why must penetrant materials for stainless steel be controlled?
faq.a: Halogens and sulfur in penetrants and cleaners can damage austenitic stainless steel and nickel alloys. Section V Article 6 limits those contaminants and the report lists the materials and their data.

faq.q: What is the temperature limit for dye penetrant inspection?
faq.a: The standard range is 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Outside it the procedure has to be qualified at the actual temperature, which matters for dark steel in direct Jacksonville summer sun.

faq.q: Is penetrant testing used on food-grade stainless tanks?
faq.a: Yes, owners sometimes examine key sanitary welds because a hairline crack can trap product and defeat cleaning. The scope sets the cleaning and final wash steps so no residue is left behind.

faq.q: How long does the penetrant stay on the surface?
faq.a: The dwell time is set in the written procedure and depends on the material, the penetrant and the flaw type being sought. It is recorded in the report along with the developer time.

faq.q: Does Atlantis supply the PT materials?
faq.a: Atlantis brings the penetrant, remover and developer needed for the job and records them by manufacturer and batch. Owners with their own approved materials list can specify it in the scope before mobilization.

faq.q: How do I get a quote for liquid penetrant testing in Jacksonville?
faq.a: Use the quote form with the parts, materials, surface condition, temperature, location, access and governing code. Atlantis has no office in Jacksonville, technicians travel to your site, and we reply within one business day.

rt.title: Radiographic Testing in Jacksonville, FL | RT Alternatives
rt.description: Atlantis does not perform radiography in the US. For Jacksonville, a UT alternative, ASNT Level III radiograph review and RT theory training are available.
rt.h1: Radiographic Testing (RT) in Jacksonville, Florida: What Atlantis Offers
rt.html:
Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing in the United States. Using a radiation source on industrial work is a licensed activity under Nuclear Regulatory Commission rules (10 CFR Part 34) or the corresponding rules of an Agreement State, and it is not a service Atlantis provides in Jacksonville or anywhere else in the country. This page describes the related services you can use if radiography was your starting point.

Ultrasonic testing in place of radiography in Jacksonville

On a busy Jacksonville terminal, shipyard or plant, clearing an exclusion zone for radiography stops neighboring work, and UT needs no such zone. Ultrasonic examination of welds looks through the weld volume with an angled beam and finds planar flaws such as lack of fusion and cracks very reliably. See the ultrasonic testing service in Jacksonville for what that involves, including Level II technicians who travel to your site.

Whether UT can stand in for RT depends on the code. ASME B31.3 and API 1104 include provisions for ultrasonic examination of production welds, AWS D1.1 gives its own ultrasonic acceptance criteria for groove welds, and ASME Section VIII allows UT in place of RT only under specific conditions. A change of method is therefore agreed with the owner, the engineer and, on code work, the authorized inspector before the job is scoped. The two methods also see different things: UT is strong on cracks and lack of fusion, while radiographs show porosity and inclusions as a picture.

Radiograph review by an ASNT Level III

Reviewing existing radiographs involves no radioactive source, so no radiation license is needed. Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, can support in three ways:

  • Independent review of radiographs, whether film or digital images, and of technique sheets, against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code.
  • A second read of disputed or borderline indications before a weld is repaired or accepted.
  • Review of a radiography contractor's procedure and written practice against the contract and the governing code.

The work is done from records and images and does not replace the radiographic examination. Owners who need the exposures made must engage a licensed radiographer of their own choice. Procedures and written practices can be written or audited through Level III consulting and written practice development.

Radiography theory courses

Radiography theory can be studied independently of any source. The radiographic testing Level 2 course covers it for people who will later work under a licensed employer. Radiation safety training and licensing are set by the regulator, and under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its own personnel. Training choices for the city are on the NDT training in Jacksonville page.

If you are weighing the options for a Jacksonville project, send the drawings, the weld list and the governing code with the request. From those, a Level III sorts the joints into those where UT is a workable route, those that still call for a radiographer you engage, and the records worth a second look before sign-off.

Surface methods and next steps in Jacksonville

For surface cracks, Atlantis also performs magnetic particle inspection and liquid penetrant testing in Jacksonville, and the Florida inspection hub lists coverage across the state. Atlantis has no office in Jacksonville; technicians travel to your site. To discuss a UT alternative, a radiograph review or training, send a request through the quote form and we reply within one business day.

faq.q: Is radiography available from Atlantis in Jacksonville?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States because it is a licensed activity under NRC or Agreement State rules. UT, radiograph review and theory training are the related services provided.

faq.q: Which welds can be examined by UT instead of RT in Jacksonville?
faq.a: That is decided by the construction code and the owner. B31.3, API 1104, AWS D1.1 and ASME Section VIII treat UT differently, so agree the change with the owner, engineer and authorized inspector beforehand.

faq.q: Does reviewing radiographs require a radiation license?
faq.a: No. Reading film or digital images and technique sheets involves no source or exposure device. An ASNT Level III compares the records with ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code.

faq.q: Will Atlantis suggest a radiography contractor for Jacksonville work?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not name or recommend radiography contractors. You choose a licensed radiographer, and Atlantis can review that contractor procedure and results if asked.

faq.q: Can I take radiography theory training through Atlantis?
faq.a: Yes, theory is covered in the radiographic testing Level 2 course. Radiation safety training and licensing come from the regulator, and the employer certifies personnel under SNT-TC-1A.
